prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current methods for mapping the functional topography of the human visual cortex rely heavily on controlled, simplified stimuli (e.g., single objects against plain backgrounds). This paradigm fails to capture the ecological complexity of natural vision, where scenes contain multiple co-occurring objects, textures, and contextual associations. While recent efforts have employed deep neural networks to predict brain activity in response to natural scenes, these approaches typically rely on global image embeddings (vectors representing the whole image). Consequently, there is a lack of methodology to determine precisely which localized sub-regions or specific semantic components within a complex, cluttered image are driving the activation of specific cortical voxels.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the spatially dense feature representations internal to modern Vision Transformers (ViTs) can be harnessed to spatially ground neural selectivity. By moving beyond the global classification token and instead leveraging the patch-level embeddings, we believe we can link voxel-wise neural activity to specific image coordinates. Furthermore, we posit that architectural artifacts in these dense features can be mitigated through a geometric consistency constraint, allowing us to generate clean "relevance maps" that identify the exact visual drivers of brain activity without requiring supervised segmentation data.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a three-stage framework to bridge dense computer vision features with neuroimaging data:

1.  **Dense Feature Extraction Strategy:** We will utilize pre-trained Vision Transformer backbones frozen in their state. Rather than pooling the output into a single vector, we will extract the feature vectors corresponding to individual spatial patches of the input image. This preserves the 2D spatial layout of the semantic information.

2.  **Learning-Free Distillation Module:** Raw dense features from self-supervised models often contain noise and spatial artifacts. To address this without training a new network, we will implement a test-time denoising procedure based on semantic consistency. We will generate multiple augmented views of the input image (using random spatial shifts and flips). These views will be passed through the backbone, and the resulting feature maps will be inversely transformed back to the original image coordinate space. By averaging these aligned features, we aim to statistically filter out inconsistent artifacts while preserving stable semantic signals.

3.  **Voxel-Wise Encoding:** We will construct a linear encoding model that maps the refined, spatially dense features directly to fMRI voxel activations. By projecting the learned weights back onto the image space, we will generate spatial attribution maps. These maps will visualize the specific regions of a natural image that positively or negatively influence the activity of a given brain voxel.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to provide a powerful tool for "semantic attribution" in systems neuroscience, enabling the dissection of high-level visual processing using ecologically valid natural scenes. Theoretically, it will allow for the unsupervised discovery of fine-grained selectivity patterns—distinguishing whether a brain region responds to a specific object category, a distinct part of an object, or low-level scene statistics (like depth or luminance)—within complex visual environments. Additionally, this method will serve as a probe to compare how different artificial vision architectures converge or diverge in their internal representation of visual semantics relative to the human brain.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted experiments to validate the "BrainSAIL" method for mapping cortical semantic selectivity using dense features from vision transformers. The experiments involved open-vocabulary segmentation tasks to validate the feature distillation method, followed by extensive fMRI encoding and analysis to map brain selectivity.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **fMRI Data:** Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD). We utilized data from 4 subjects (S1, S2, S5, S7) who completed the full scan of 10,000 images (subset of COCO images). Each image was viewed 3 times.
    *   **Data Splits:** Training set consisted of approximately 9,000 unique images per subject. The test set consisted of approximately 1,000 shared images viewed by all subjects.
    *   **Segmentation Validation Datasets:** ADE20k, COCO Object, COCO Stuff, and VOC20.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Segmentation:** Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and Pearson correlation.
    *   **Brain Encoding:** $R^2$ (coefficient of determination) on held-out test data.
    *   **Alignment/Selectivity:** Percentage of top-activating images aligned with text-based category prompts.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Feature Extraction/Smoothing:** SCLIP, NACLIP (compared against NACLIP + Learning-Free Distillation).
    *   **Brain Encoder Backbones:**
        *   CLIP (OpenAI ViT-B/16, contrastive image-text).
        *   DINO (Meta DINOv2 ViT-B/14 + registers, self-supervised image-only).
        *   SigLIP (NVIDIA RADIOv2.5 ViT-B/16, pairwise non-contrastive image-text).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Experiments utilized a mixture of GPUs including Nvidia V100 (16GB/32GB), 2080 Ti, A6000, 6000Ada, L40S, and 4090.
    *   **Optimization:** Adam optimizer with decoupled weight decay of $2 \times 10^{-2}$.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial rate of $3 \times 10^{-4}$, decaying exponentially to $1.5 \times 10^{-4}$ over 100 epochs.
    *   **Loss Function:** MSE loss.
    *   **Image Processing:**
        *   CLIP resized to $224 \times 224$.
        *   DINO resized to $518 \times 518$.
        *   SigLIP resized to $768 \times 768$.
        *   Augmentations: Random pixel-wise value scaling (0.95–1.05), random horizontal/vertical offsets (up to 4 pixels), independent Gaussian noise ($\mu=0, \sigma^2=0.05$).
    *   **Distillation:** We utilized a learning-free distillation module. For CLIP, we used 51 augmentation steps. For DINO and SigLIP, we used 25 augmentation steps.
    *   **Voxel Selection:** Subject native space voxels (1.8mm resolution). Cortical voxels selected based on the `nsdgeneral` mask.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Methodological Validation**
*   We observed that raw dense embeddings from contrastive models (specifically CLIP with NACLIP adapter) contained significant artifacts and noise.
*   Applying the learning-free distillation module (averaging over augmentations) removed these artifacts, resulting in clean, spatially dense embeddings localized to relevant semantic components.
*   The distillation process achieved state-of-the-art results for open-vocabulary CLIP-based segmentation on the datasets tested.

**Brain Region Localization and Factorization**
*   Using UMAP dimensionality reduction on the learned brain encoder weights, we observed that the functional topology of the brain factorized along axes corresponding to "people," "scenes," and "food."
*   We found that place regions (RSC, OPA, PPA) showed selectivity for scene components.
*   We found that people regions (EBA, FFA, OFA) showed selectivity for face and body parts.
*   We identified food-responsive regions flanking the FFA that strongly corresponded to food in natural images.
*   The method successfully localized objects relevant to category-selective brain regions for the top-activating images (e.g., localizing faces in face regions, buildings in place regions).
*   We noted that the "Word" region exhibited cross-selectivity to faces and food.

**Feature Correlates (Depth, Saturation, Luminance)**
*   **Depth:** We observed that scene-selective regions (RSC, PPA, and OPA) all exhibited a preference for high depth.
*   **Saturation:** We identified two stripes on the ventral surface of each hemisphere, surrounding the FFA, that showed a preference for high color saturation. These locations correspond to known food-selective regions.
*   **Luminance:** We observed an anterior/posterior split in the OPA; one subregion preferred high color luminance (brightness), while the other preferred low color luminance. This corresponds to previously identified outdoor/indoor selectivity splits.

**Comparison of Foundation Model Backbones**
*   **Predictive Performance:** We observed that CLIP, DINO, and SigLIP backbones all achieved high and comparable $R^2$ performance on the fMRI test set. However, CLIP and SigLIP (language-supervised) achieved slightly higher performance than DINO (image-only self-supervision).
*   **Representational Similarity:** Relevance maps generated by CLIP and SigLIP were more similar to each other than either was to DINO.
*   **Semantic vs. Visual Selectivity:**
    *   DINO-based maps demonstrated greater sensitivity to low-level visual features (e.g., color, texture) rather than high-level semantic concepts.
    *   For example, in food-responsive regions, DINO maps for a pizza image excluded toppings and missed differently colored vegetables, appearing to focus on the texture/color of the crust/plate.
    *   In face regions, DINO maps showed less reliance on semantic facial features (eyes, nose, mouth) compared to CLIP and SigLIP.
    *   We attributed this to DINO's lack of language supervision, which seemingly prevents it from learning high-level semantic correlations linking visually disparate parts of a category.

For each quartet of images, the content is as follows – Top left: Original RGB image; Top right: Dimension reduction of BrainSAIL embeddings for the image; Bottom: Two text queries using CLIP text branch showing language-indicated relevance results. (c) UMAP results on an inflated view of the brain for S1. (d) UMAP results on cortical flatmaps for S2, S5 and S7. These results demonstrate that BrainSAIL can effectively localize semantically meaningful components of natural images and map them to appropriate brain regions. The cortical maps show color-coded mappings that align well with functionally-defined regions: body regions (EBA), face regions (FFA/aTL-faces), place regions (RSC/OPA/PPA), and food regions (yellow). Note that the food regions have been identified as flanking FFA by Jain et al. (2023), but we do not have independent functional localizer data for food for these subjects.

While all models show broadly similar feature relevance for a given brain area, there are important differences. DINO, with no language supervision, exhibits greater sensitivity to visual similarity, at the cost of semantic coherence.
--------------------------------------------------

  - Caption: Figure 7: Model similarity across ROIs. Brain encoder backbone spatial similarity for the ground truth top-100 images from the test set for each category-selective brain region. A ⋆ denotes a domaindefined network of regions encompassing multiple ROIs. CLIP and SigLIP relevance maps are more similar to one another than either is to DINO. Error bars indicate standard error across the 100 images.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_1.png
  - Caption: Figure 1: The BrainSAIL framework leverages dense visual features. (a) An fMRI encoder learns a map from images to voxel-wise activations in the brain. Encoders leveraging frozen foundation models based on vision transformers (ViTs) with voxel-wise adapters are currently the highest accuracy models for brain prediction (Conwell et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a). (b) Given an image and a ViT backbone for the fMRI encoder, we modify the backbone to output dense features. The dense backbone is wrapped inside of a Learning-Free Distillation Module. This module takes an image I and 2D image coordinates C, and generates transformed images and coordinates (Ii, Ci) for a given transform θi. The dense features and transformed coordinates are provided to a denoising module to generate clean dense features. The frozen voxel-wise adapter from (a) is applied to each patch to generate dense relevance maps which highlight the image regions activating the voxel. (c) Using CLIP ViT-B/16 with the latest NACLIP adapter, we show relevance maps using the CLIP text encoder. The NACLIP raw features are highly noisy and contain artifacts, while the distilled features are localized to the relevant semantic components with high accuracy. Note that we achieve state-of-the-art open vocabulary CLIP-based segmentation results using our method.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4: Grounding results using BrainSAIL. We visualize the top test set images as predicted by the CLIP fMRI encoder for each category selective region. For each image, we also visualize the image-wise UMAP for the distilled dense features. Note the UMAP basis here is computed imagewise, and not shared with Figure 3. The image-wise UMAP shows the semantic components present in the dense features. For each image, we further visualize the feature relevancy map for the category selective voxels illustrating that this method extracts the semantically relevant regions in complex compositional images.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 6:
  - Filename: figure_5.png
  - Caption: Figure 5: Feature correlates with BrainSAIL. We visualize the depth, color saturation, and color luminance (brightness) correlates for each brain region using BrainSAIL . (a) The scene selective regions, retrosplenial cortex (RSC), parahippocampal place area (PPA), and occipital place area (OPA) are all identified as having a preference for high depth. (b) On the ventral surface, we identify two stripes on each hemisphere, surrounding FFA with high saturation preference. These are the same brain regions identified by Jain et al. (2023) as being food selective. (c) In OPA, we identify an anterior/posterior split, where one region has high color luminance preference, and the other has low color luminance preference. This are the same regions identified by Luo et al. (2023) as being outdoor/indoor selective.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 7:
  - Filename: figure_6.png
  - Caption: Figure 6: Comparing the brain prediction performance for different encoder backbones. (a) We validate each encoder R2 on a test set and find that all three models achieve very high performance (comparable to Wang et al. (2023a)). (b) The voxel-wise correlation of test set R2 for the three models. CLIP and SigLIP, which rely on language supervision, achieve higher performance than DINO (which trained via self-supervision with images).
--------------------------------------------------
Item 8:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2: The Learning-Free Distillation Module. (a) Given an image, we generate image-space coordinates (u, v) for each pixel. We then randomly sample from θ1...n, where θi has vertical/horizontal offset, and left-right flips. The augmented images are provided to a frozen backbone with dense adapter. The features are projected to the original image space via an inverse transform T −1(θi). (b) UMAP visualization of the dense features. The same fitted basis is used for both visualizations. (c) With CLIP, we can perform zero-shot text queries. Note the artifacts above the bird’s head. In practice artifact location is different for each image. The distilled results are significantly better.
--------------------------------------------------

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}

```

### Example Code for Tables

```latex
\label{sample-table}

\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Understanding how the human brain processes visual information from natural experience remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While functional mapping studies have successfully identified cortical regions preferential to specific categories (e.g., faces, places, bodies) using simplified, isolated stimuli, this approach fails to capture the complexity of the real world. Natural visual experiences involve rich scenes with co-occurring objects, textures, and contextual associations.

Current state-of-the-art brain encoding models leverage large-scale artificial neural networks (ANNs) to predict neural responses. However, these models typically operate on **whole-image embeddings**, treating the stimulus as a monolithic vector. This creates a critical resolution gap: when a voxel responds to a complex natural image, we cannot currently determine which specific region or semantic component of that image drove the response. We lack a methodology to spatially decompose neural selectivity within the clutter of naturalistic scenes without relying on restrictive, hand-crafted stimuli.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that we can disentangle the image-level visual drivers of neural tuning by unifying the latent spaces of whole-image embeddings and **dense visual features**. We propose **BrainSAIL** (Semantic Attribution and Image Localization), a framework that leverages the internal representations of pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViTs).

Our core premise is that while contrastive models (like CLIP) are trained on global objectives, their internal patch-level representations contain rich, albeit noisy, spatial semantic information. By introducing a novel **Learning-Free Distillation Module**, we can denoise these dense features to generate clean, spatially resolved embeddings. By mapping these dense features to voxel activations, we will be able to generate "relevance maps" that isolate the specific subregions of an image responsible for driving selectivity in higher visual cortex, effectively grounding neural selectivity in the pixels of natural images.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a three-stage pipeline: (1) An image-to-brain encoding framework based on ViT backbones, (2) A method for extracting dense features from these backbones, and (3) A learning-free distillation algorithm to refine these features for spatial attribution.

### 1. Image-to-Brain Encoder Formulation
We will model the voxel-wise encoding function $F_\phi$ that predicts fMRI activations $B \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N}$, where $N$ is the number of voxels. The encoder will be conditioned on an input image $\mathcal{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$.

The architecture will utilize a frozen Vision Foundation Model backbone $G(\mathcal{T})$ which outputs an embedding vector of dimension $\mathbb{R}^{1 \times M}$. We will employ a per-voxel adapter, parameterized as a linear probe with weights $W \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$ and bias $b \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times N}$. The prediction is formulated as:

$$
\hat{B} = \left[ \frac { \mathbf { G } _ { \mathrm { i m g } } ( \mathcal { T } ) } { \| \mathbf { G } _ { \mathrm { i m g } } ( \mathcal { T } ) \| _ { 2 } } \times W + b \right]
$$

We will support multiple backbones, specifically **CLIP (ViT-B/16)**, **DINOv2**, and **SigLIP**.

### 2. Deriving Dense Features from ViT Backbones
Standard ViTs trained on contrastive objectives supervise a global `[CLS]` token, often leaving spatial patch tokens noisy or artifact-prone. To extract meaningful dense features, we will modify the final self-attention (SA) block of the ViT.

Let $(q_i, k_i, v_i)$ be the query, key, and value features for image patch $i$, with $m$ total spatial patches. We will implement modified attention mechanisms, such as **NACLIP** or **MaskCLIP**. For instance, using a spatial attentive bias $\omega$, the output for a patch $j$ ($Out_j$) is defined as:

$$
\mathrm { O u t . N A } _ { j } = f \left( \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { m } \left[ \mathrm { softmax } \left( \frac { q _ { j } q ^ { T } + \omega _ { j } } { C } \right) _ { j } \cdot v _ { k } \right] \right)
$$

where $C$ is a scaling constant and $f$ denotes the function applied to the token after the last self-attention.

### 3. Learning-Free Feature Distillation Module
Raw dense embeddings from models like CLIP often contain high-frequency artifacts. To resolve this without training a separate segmentation network, we propose a distillation module based on the geometric consistency of semantic features.

**Algorithm:**
We define an augmentation function that applies horizontal/vertical offsets $(u, v)$ and horizontal flips. For an image $\mathcal{T}$ and coordinate grid $\mathcal{C}$, we generate $n$ augmented views via parameters $\theta_{1...n}$.

Let $M$ be the ViT model with the dense adapter. The distillation process is:
1.  Initialize accumulator tensors $Q$ (features) and $K$ (counts).
2.  For each augmentation $i \in \{1...n\}$:
    *   Transform inputs: $(\mathcal{T}_i, \mathcal{C}_i) = \text{Augment}(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \theta_i)$.
    *   Extract noisy dense features: $F_i = M(\mathcal{T}_i)$.
    *   Inverse transform features to original coordinates: $(F_i^{valid}, \mathcal{C}_i^{valid}) = \text{InverseAugment}(F_i, \mathcal{C}_i, \theta_i)$.
    *   Accumulate: $Q[\mathcal{C}_i^{valid}] \leftarrow Q[\mathcal{C}_i^{valid}] + F_i^{valid}$.
3.  Output mean features: $Q / K$.

**Mathematical Justification:**
We formulate this averaging as extracting the optimal embedding $\vec{p^*}$ under a Mean Squared Error (MSE) objective. Let $\vec{p_i}$ be the feature candidate for a specific patch under augmentation $i$:

$$
\Vec { p ^ { * } } = \underset { \hat { p } } { \mathrm { min } } \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \lVert \Vec { p _ { i } } - \hat { p } \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \right)
$$

Expanding this term:

$$
= \underset { \hat { p } } { \mathrm { min } } \left( n \cdot \hat { p } ^ { T } \hat { p } - 2 \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \Vec { p _ { i } } ^ { T } \hat { p } ) \right)
$$

The solution to this objective is $\vec{p^*} = \frac{1}{n} \sum \vec{p_i}$. This process filters out non-consistent artifacts while preserving semantic signals that are equivariant to shifts and flips. Finally, we will apply the trained voxel-wise adapters (from Step 1) to these distilled dense patch features to produce spatial **relevance maps**.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Dense Semantic Grounding:** We will provide the first method capable of projecting the semantic selectivity of high-level visual cortex onto specific pixels of natural images, moving beyond whole-image analysis.
2.  **Unsupervised Segmentation of Selectivity:** By leveraging the inherent structure of foundation models, this method will allow us to decompose complex scenes into "neural relevance maps" (e.g., separating face-selective pixels from background-selective pixels) without requiring pixel-level supervision or manual annotation.
3.  **High-Throughput Feature Characterization:** BrainSAIL will enable large-scale interrogation of the visual cortex, allowing us to map selectivity for not only high-level categories but also low-level statistics (depth, luminance, saturation) across thousands of natural images.
4.  **Model Interrogation:** The framework will serve as a tool to compare different vision foundation models (e.g., contrastive vs. non-contrastive), revealing how different training objectives influence the spatial localization of features that align with human brain activity.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
